items.t: Prophylaxis of systemic embolism in rheumatic heart disease and atrial fibrillation; prophylaxis after prosthetic heart valve insertion; prophylaxis and treatment of venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism; transient cerebral ischaemic attacks.

items.t: Give every patient a patient-held information booklet ('warfarin card') and explain which symptoms need medical attention.

src.q: Patients should be given a patient-held information booklet ('warfarin card') and informed of symptoms for which they should seek medical attention.

items.t: Adults (all indications): typical induction 10 mg daily for 2 days, tailored to the individual; usual maintenance 3 to 9 mg once daily at the same time each day, adjusted to prothrombin time/INR.

src.q: The typical induction dose is 10mg daily for 2 days but this should be tailored to individual requirements.
The daily maintenance dose is usually 3 to 9mg taken at the same time each day.

items.t: Emergencies: start heparin and warfarin together; stop heparin at least six hours before the first control test.

src.q: In emergencies, anticoagulant therapy should be initiated with heparin and warfarin together.
should be discontinued at least six hours before the first test is carried out

items.t: Elderly: as for adults but the dose may need to be lower.

src.q: Elderly: As for adults, but dosage may need to be lowered.

items.t: Protein C deficiency: start without a loading dose (even with heparin); protein S deficiency: start slowly.

src.q: In patients with protein C deficiency, therapy should be introduced without a loading dose of warfarin even if heparin is given.

items.t: Any condition where bleeding risk may outweigh the benefit of anticoagulation.

src.q: Anticoagulation is contraindicated in any physical condition in which the risk of haemorrhage might be greater that the potential clinical benefits of anticoagulation

items.t: Bleeding is the most frequent adverse effect. Give with caution where there is a risk of serious haemorrhage (e.g. NSAID use, recent ischaemic stroke, bacterial endocarditis, previous GI bleeding). Risk factors include INR >4.0, age ≥65, variable INRs, uncontrolled hypertension, cerebrovascular disease, falls risk, anaemia, malignancy, renal insufficiency, interacting drugs.

src.q: Warfarin should be given with caution to patients where there is a risk of serious haemorrhage (e.g. concomitant NSAID use, recent ischaemic stroke, bacterial endocarditis, previous gastrointestinal bleeding)
Risk factors for bleeding include high intensity of anticoagulation (INR >4.0), age ≥65, highly variable INRs

items.t: Active peptic ulcer: treat with caution, review regularly and teach how to recognise bleeding.

src.q: Due to a high risk of bleeding, patients with active peptic ulcers should be treated with caution.

items.t: Ischaemic stroke: a break is justified; restart 2-14 days after, depending on infarct size and blood pressure; stop for 14 days with large embolic stroke or uncontrolled hypertension.

src.q: Warfarin treatment should be re-started 2-14 days following ischaemic stroke, depending on the size of the infarct and blood pressure.

items.t: Surgery: no severe bleeding risk - operate with INR <2.5. Severe bleeding risk - stop warfarin 3 days before. If warfarin cannot be stopped 3 days before, reverse with low-dose vitamin K. Routine dental surgery (e.g. extraction) does not need warfarin stopped.

src.q: For surgery where there is a risk of severe bleeding, warfarin should be stopped 3 days prior to surgery.
anticoagulation should be reversed with low-dose vitamin K
Warfarin need not be stopped before routine dental surgery, eg, tooth extraction.

items.t: Thyroid disorders: hyper- or hypothyroidism changes warfarin metabolism; monitor closely when starting.

src.q: patients with hyper- or hypo-thyroidism should be closely monitored on starting warfarin therapy

items.t: Protein C deficiency: risk of skin necrosis on starting; start without loading dose.

src.q: Patients with protein C deficiency are at risk of developing skin necrosis when starting warfarin treatment.

items.t: Calciphylaxis (rare): consider stopping warfarin if diagnosed; reported also with normal renal function.

src.q: In case calciphylaxis is diagnosed, appropriate treatment should be started and consideration should be given to stopping treatment with warfarin.
cases have been reported in patients taking warfarin, including those with normal renal function

items.t: Anticoagulant-related nephropathy: acute kidney injury possible, linked to excessive anticoagulation and haematuria; close monitoring including renal function if supratherapeutic INR with haematuria.

src.q: Close monitoring including renal function evaluation is advised in patients with a supratherapeutic INR and hematuria (including microscopic).

items.t: CYP2C9 and VKORC1 genetic variability can significantly affect dose needs.

src.q: Genetic variability particularly in relation to CYP2C9 and VKORC1 can significantly affect dose requirements for warfarin.

items.t: BUMPS: avoided in pregnancy where possible (birth defects); may sometimes be recommended with mechanical heart valves. Do not stop without specialist advice; people with a metal valve need urgent specialist advice within a day or two of a positive test.

src.q: Warfarin is avoided in pregnancy where possible as it can cause birth defects.

items.t: SmPC: can be used during breastfeeding; no effects expected at therapeutic doses.

src.q: Warfarin can be used during breast-feeding.

items.t: Life-threatening haemorrhage: stop warfarin, give prothrombin complex concentrate 30-50 units/kg (or FFP 15 mL/kg if none); discuss with haematologist/NPIS. Non-life-threatening: slow IV phytomenadione 10-20 mg (adults).
